cells.tense: The work is in your hands right now, at whatever depth it has reached.
cells.act: refine one distinction by close attention
cells.ask: Choose one plant, one skill, one piece at the bench, and stay with it slowly past the first pass — deeper than the once-over you usually give. Nothing else gets a turn today.
cells.core: You can tend a living thing toward depth. The young tree gets watered on the days it shows no change, the technique gets its repetitions when nobody is watching, and you stay long enough that it becomes real. That patience is the thing itself, not the waiting around it. Something in your care is at that stage now, further along than it appears. There is a way of being alone with the work that connects you to it rather than hiding you from people — that is the version of solitude worth keeping. This is attention that sharpens what it looks at instead of tightening around it. What it feeds next is yours to choose. The craft deepens without being worried into depth.
cells.sheetLine: You tend it until it has roots.
cells.verb: building one structure by hand until it is deeper than the last pass
cells.place: in the garden where something you started is still growing

cells.tense: You are bracing for the season when this finally grows into what you meant it to be.
cells.act: mark the good thing together, the day it happens
cells.ask: When something in your care comes good — a batch, a plant, a person's step — say so out loud while it is still that same day. A sentence is enough.
cells.core: In the garden where your care is growing, you already stand in a future where the thing is finished, measuring each day against it. More effort goes in earlier than the growth has asked for; the next stage gets forced while this one is still soft. The patience has turned to pressure, and the ones you tend may be handed a version of it they didn't ask for. That is the excess, and it points somewhere useful. Let the gladness reach the others. Sharing what has actually happened, on the day it happens, puts you back where the growth is — today, at its real size. What gets marked keeps its own timing.

cells.tense: A door to this closed a while back, and you are at the place where it used to be.
cells.act: put the frame on the table before anyone asks
cells.ask: Say once, plainly, how you want this to go. Name the shape before anyone asks you for it. Then leave it where it lands.
cells.core: You watch others plant and tend, and your own hands stay still. A decision made earlier, or something that ended, is where your attention keeps returning. The care has not gone anywhere — you feel it whenever a thing grows near you. It simply isn't being spent on anything, and watching won't restart it. Saying what you want out loud does. Claim one small structure in the open — how this piece should go, stated once, no argument after — and it stops belonging to whoever else has an opinion. The order you state is yours, and it makes sense the moment it leaves your mouth. The hands come back after the voice does.
cells.sheetLine: You're at a door that shut some time ago.
cells.verb: building one structure by hand until it is deeper than the last pass

cells.tense: You are keeping this alive and speaking about it as though it keeps itself.
cells.act: move at the pace your feeling can sustain
cells.ask: Work the piece you're tending at a speed that feels steady in your body — not the surge, not the catch-up. No finish line. Just the pace that holds.
cells.core: Ask anyone nearby who keeps the plants alive and the work going, and the answer points at you. The watering happens because you remember it; the practice holds because you return to it. But you tell it as if the thing simply grew, and from that telling the garden looks self-running while your hands are the ones in the soil. That is the practice speaking as terrain, and it makes your part disappear. Feel where the care actually comes from and give it the speed it can hold. When the rhythm is one the weeks allow, the will and the want move the same direction instead of you dragging one behind the other. Then the structure stands because you say it does, not because it got lucky.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it alive and call it nature taking its course.
